title: How scientists see science

paragraphs.text: Of what value to scientists is the philosophy of science? It is certainly of value if it causes us to question our basic assumptions, or even to realise which unstated assumptions we have been operating under.

Distinguished philosopher of science Philip Kitcher tells us in Science, Truth, and Democracy that we scientists are realists: we believe that there is a real world and that science can figure out how it all works. To Kitcher, this is an extreme view, just as unacceptable as its opposite: that there is no such thing as truth, and science is a belief system no better than any other. But Kitcher adopts a position that is closer to the scientists' view than to its opposite. There is a real world out there, he believes, and science is able to discover important truths about it; the key, he thinks, is the word 'important'.

Important to whom, and for what purpose? He argues that there can be no objective way of deciding. The only reasonable approach, he believes, is to assume that scientific truths are important if their fruits are beneficial. Thus the practice of science for its own sake is not an absolute good, but must be judged by the benefits that arise from it, provided those benefits are distributed fairly. In this way, science could become invaluable. He concludes that the decisions that set the agenda for science should be made democratically, with the informed cooperation of every segment of society. The elaborate means by which that cooperation would be carried out he calls 'well-ordered science'.

Kitcher takes the following approach to writing: he likes to argue by setting out extremes, deciding that neither is correct, and concluding that the truth must lie somewhere in the middle. This technique makes him seem eminently reasonable, no matter how far off the real path he occasionally leads us. Kitcher contrasts 'well-ordered science' with alternative ways of setting the scientific agenda. At one extreme is what he calls 'internal elitism', in which scientists make all the decisions. In reality, however, decisions are made by scientists together with a privileged group of outsiders who have the funds to support research. This (the status quo) Kitcher calls 'external elitism', which is under constant pressure from scientists who want to convert it to internal elitism.

At the opposite extreme from internal elitism is 'vulgar democracy', which attempts to satisfy citizens' preferences by giving priority to projects that are believed to be favored by a majority of people—an approach with the obvious deficiency that it could result in 'a tyranny of the ignorant'. The best alternative to either extreme, Kitcher proposes, is 'enlightened democracy', in which decisions would be made by groups representing every segment of society, after being tutored by scientists. This is a condensed version of the more elaborate deliberations of 'well-ordered science'. This approach may seem entirely reasonable to those who have never explained to non-scientists what science is about, but from experience, I can say it is often a futile struggle.

The issues that seem to motivate Kitcher's arguments are seen most clearly in the biomedical arena. The National Institute of Health (NIH) in the US habitually expands its budget, with the argument that the research it supports benefits the health and well-being of all. Kitcher analyses a 1998 committee report addressing the charge that the NIH is more interested in satisfying the curiosity of scientists than in improving patient care. Although the report did call for more public input, it also defended the current situation, saying that the NIH has produced an 'accumulation of basic knowledge about human biology that is unparalleled in the history of science'. Kitcher agrees, but points out that the NIH has also received a level of funding that is unparalleled in the history of science.

Of course it is not only biology which asks for public money and promises to contribute to public welfare. In order to procure funding to pursue whatever we scientists find interesting, many of us have adopted the embarrassing habit of claiming that our research will produce material benefits. And we have produced the material benefits almost in spite of ourselves.

Physicist Richard Feynman was disdainful of philosophers of science, but he was nevertheless capable of deep insights. Many years ago, he and I had long discussions on the central question of Kitcher's thesis: what makes something important in science? The key, Feynman decided, lay in choosing important problems to work on. An important problem, he believed, is one where the solution turns out not only to solve the problem at hand but also to shed new light on the solutions to other problems as well.

Admittedly, on first hearing this formulation, I found it rather mysterious, but since then I have seen scientists putting Feynman's theory into practice. The capacity to choose such problems is what we might call scientific good taste. Some scientists seem to possess it naturally and others don't. Democracy has nothing to do with it.

Kitcher's book has made me think about my basic assumptions, but it has not made me change them. Unlike Kitcher, I do not fear the unfettered search for truth. We don't know in advance what results scientific research will produce but some scientists instinctively ask the most important questions. Our system of decision-making, imperfect as it is, tends to identify those individuals and give them the resources they need. I remain, therefore, a realist and an 'internal elitist', yielding reluctantly to external elitism when I need more funding. I believe that is preferable in relation to governing the business of science, rather than Kitcher's ideal of 'well-ordered science’.
